articles.title: Breaking the silence: Pratishta’s journey from childhood abuse to advocacy
articles.summary: Across South Asia, including Nepal, survivors of rape and child sexual abuse face not only violence but also victim-blaming social norms that perpetuate stigma, silence and impunity.
articles.content:
Editorial note: This article contains mention of gender-based violence, sexual assault, violence against children, and child sexual abuse, which may be triggering for some readers.

November 25 to December 10, 2026, marks the UN’s 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence. However, even as gender-based violence gets more recognition globally, survivors are still struggling to access social or legal justice. South Asia is no exception to this. Global Voices sat down with one survivor of childhood abuse who uses her experience to fuel her advocacy work today.

South Asia is home to nearly one quarter of the world’s population, woven with a diverse, culture-driven fabric where women are often celebrated as goddesses. However, this veneration doesn’t necessarily mean South Asian women are safe or free from abuse.

In Nepal, there are far too many examples of crimes against women and girls. For instance, Nirmala Panta, 13, was found dead in a sugarcane field — a case which has remained unsolved since 2018. Bhagirathi Bhatta, 17, was choked to death when returning home from school in 2021, and Inisha BK, 16, was found unconscious in the Janagaran Community Forest in Surkhet in early 2026. A similar yet shocking case is that of a 3-year-old Garima, who was found dead inside an abandoned house in Jeetpur in southern Nepal. While these tragic rape and murder cases leave deep scars in Nepal’s national psyche, even more cases go unheard and unreported.

Sparking a nationwide outrage, such cases force the country to confront a collective shame. They raise questions around human morality, diminishing trust and affection in society, and breakdowns in the legal justice system. In the face of these atrocities, women took to the streets, demanding justice and accountability. But their calls fell on deaf ears.

Pratistha Gautam’s story

“I was 11 years old when I was sexually abused by my close maternal uncle for four days,” said Pratishtha Gautam in an online interview with Global Voices in November 2026. Opening up about this incident was a real challenge for her, yet she was committed to sharing her story.

Her childhood was by no means easy. She moved regularly as a child, and at seven years old, she was sent to her maternal uncle’s house for a year because her parents had to move away to address her younger brother’s health issues.

It was in this house that a monster took away her innocence.

After four days of abuse, she escaped on the fifth day with the help of her neighbors. Finally getting a chance to flee from her abuser, she “rushed to my room, quickly happened to lock the door by chance, thankfully, and began to scream out to my neighbors.” She had witnessed men mistreating women in her neighborhood growing up and feels lucky that her cries weren’t met with indifference.

She felt neglected growing up and believed her parents loved her younger brother more. This left her with a sense of detachment from her family. The abuse only compounded her challenges. As she says, “It was not easy at all.”

The experience has left her with scars: “I have been awakened with nightmares since that incident, making my sleep extremely difficult.” She also suffers from panic attacks when she sees material about sexual abuse. She describes feeling like her heart is swollen and being torn apart. When triggered, she often freezes up and dissociates.

According to research from the American Academy of Pediatrics journal, child sexual abuse can be incredibly detrimental to a person’s long-term mental well-being. Child abuse survivors are more likely to suffer from anxiety disorders, depression, eating disorders and disturbances, sleep disruption and insomnia, and dissociation, as well as adverse physical health conditions and attachment issues, according to the Center of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse.

This highlights the immense scale of pain that many children experience when they are victims of sexual abuse. Not everyone is able to speak out about such abuses. This is particularly true in South Asia, where there is a social stigma around abuse, due to entrenched ideas around “purity.”

She resents suggestions that it is women’s responsibility to not “tempt” men or draw attention to themselves. “Why should we be the ones to cover ourselves up?” she asks. She refuses to hide and stay silent while her abuser “is living free somewhere.” She refuses to remain invisible.

Even as many countries make strides in gender equality, gender-based violence continues to be a major issue. In a 2023 report, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that nearly one in three (31.6 percent) of women worldwide have been subjected to either physical and/or sexual violence in their lifetime — roughly 840 million women and girls.

At the root of gender-based violence lies a belief in male superiority. Not all men would openly endorse this belief, yet many see themselves as protectors of the women in their lives: their sisters, mothers, girlfriends, and wives. But this notion of protection is deeply flawed, especially when it comes at the cost of women’s freedom, mobility, access to opportunities, dreams, and agency.

Gautam recognizes this notion in her own upbringing. She had dreams of her own and was ready to chase them, but her family had a different plan for her. They wanted “to get me married off,” she said. She kept her independence through stubbornness and determination.

A trauma that persists

Today, Gautam lives in Adelaide in South Australia. She suffers from complex PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) and works as a mental health clinician helping other survivors of abuse. She reflected, in a heavy tone, on being a thousand miles away from home but safe and independent.

PTSD and insomnia aren’t the only consequences of her abuse. While she was once married, she struggled to cope with her trauma, and it negatively impacted her relationship, eventually leading to divorce.

As part of her treatment, Gautam has met regularly with psychotherapists over the years. Eventually, even that wasn’t enough. She put everything on hold for a year and gave herself time and space to focus on her mental health. She believes she would have difficulty living a normal life and still struggles with relationships. “I hate men. I used to hate them and still have trust issues,” she said.

Even as she struggles to process her own trauma, she also works to help others recover from abuse and offers pro bono psychological counseling. Being part of the solution has in some ways helped her heal. Her passion as a mental health clinician goes beyond her own individual experiences to the collective — a reminder to be empathetic as humans first.

While she primarily works in Australia, she is also committed to helping women back in her home country of Nepal. She has collaborated with Rakshya Nepal, an organization in Nepal that protects women and girls from sexual exploitation and trafficking.

Reflecting back on the choices she made, she said, “I cannot imagine if I could afford this luxury of mental space if I were not in Australia.”

This is also a testament to how South Asia treats survivors of sexual and physical abuse — even if they gather the courage to speak the truth, too often they are met with judgment and scorn. Part of this is due to limited regard for mental health, but it’s also about entrenched gender roles and strong societal expectations. There is a popular saying in Nepal reflecting these persistent gender dynamics: “timi ta chori manche ho ni” and “chora manche vayera gari halchan ni,” which roughly translates to “you are a girl, and boys will be boys.”
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the inspiring journey of a survivor of childhood sexual abuse who has transformed her trauma into advocacy and mental health support for others, addressing a significant social issue of gender-based violence and stigma in South Asia. It focuses on a real-world impact with broad societal relevance, emphasizing mental health, justice, and empowerment for survivors, thus meeting the criteria for good news.
articles.personality_title: From pain to purpose: A survivor’s fight against abuse and stigma in Nepal
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In South Asia, many survivors of sexual abuse face not only violence but also blame and silence from society. This makes it hard for them to get justice or support. Nepal has seen many tragic cases of violence against girls and women, sparking public outrage but little change.

**What happened** – Pratistha Gautam, a woman from Nepal, was sexually abused by a family member when she was 11. Despite the trauma, she escaped and later moved to Australia. Today, she works as a mental health clinician, helping other survivors of abuse. She also supports organizations in Nepal that protect women and girls.

**Impact** – Pratistha’s story shows how survivors can turn their pain into action. She helps others heal by offering counseling and raising awareness about abuse and mental health. Her work challenges harmful social ideas that blame victims and keeps people silent. By speaking out, she fights stigma and encourages change in attitudes toward survivors.

**What's next step** – Pratistha plans to continue her mental health work in Australia and Nepal. Her efforts may inspire more survivors to seek help and speak openly. This could lead to better support systems and stronger voices against gender-based violence in South Asia.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Pratistha Gautam’s journey from abuse to advocacy highlights the power of courage and care in helping survivors heal and fight stigma.
articles.personality_title_fr: De la douleur à l'engagement : Le combat d'une survivante contre les abus et la stigmatisation au Népal
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Asie du Sud, de nombreuses survivantes d'abus sexuels font face non seulement à la violence, mais aussi au blâme et au silence de la société. Cela rend difficile l'accès à la justice ou au soutien. Le Népal a connu plusieurs cas tragiques de violences contre les filles et les femmes, provoquant une indignation publique mais peu de changements.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Pratistha Gautam, une femme originaire du Népal, a été victime d'abus sexuels par un membre de sa famille à l'âge de 11 ans. Malgré ce traumatisme, elle a réussi à s’échapper et a émigré en Australie. Aujourd'hui, elle travaille comme clinicienne en santé mentale, aidant d'autres survivantes d'abus. Elle soutient aussi des organisations au Népal qui protègent les femmes et les filles.

**Impact** – L'histoire de Pratistha montre comment les survivantes peuvent transformer leur douleur en action. Elle aide les autres à guérir en offrant des conseils et en sensibilisant sur les abus et la santé mentale. Son travail remet en question les idées nuisibles qui blâment les victimes et maintiennent le silence. En parlant ouvertement, elle combat la stigmatisation et encourage un changement d'attitude envers les survivantes.

**Prochaine étape** – Pratistha prévoit de poursuivre son travail en santé mentale en Australie et au Népal. Ses efforts pourraient inspirer davantage de survivantes à chercher de l’aide et à s’exprimer. Cela pourrait conduire à de meilleurs systèmes de soutien et à des voix plus fortes contre la violence basée sur le genre en Asie du Sud.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Le parcours de Pratistha Gautam, de la victime à l'activiste, montre le pouvoir du courage et du soutien pour aider les survivantes à guérir et à lutter contre la stigmatisation.
articles.personality_title_es: De dolor a propósito: La lucha de una sobreviviente contra el abuso y el estigma en Nepal
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En el sur de Asia, muchas sobrevivientes de abuso sexual enfrentan no solo violencia, sino también culpa y silencio por parte de la sociedad. Esto dificulta que obtengan justicia o apoyo. Nepal ha vivido varios casos trágicos de violencia contra niñas y mujeres, que han provocado indignación pública pero pocos cambios.

**Qué pasó** – Pratistha Gautam, una mujer de Nepal, fue abusada sexualmente por un familiar cuando tenía 11 años. A pesar del trauma, logró escapar y se mudó a Australia. Hoy trabaja como clínica de salud mental, ayudando a otras sobrevivientes de abuso. También apoya organizaciones en Nepal que protegen a mujeres y niñas.

**Impacto** – La historia de Pratistha muestra cómo las sobrevivientes pueden convertir su dolor en acción. Ella ayuda a otros a sanar ofreciendo consejería y creando conciencia sobre el abuso y la salud mental. Su trabajo desafía las ideas dañinas que culpan a las víctimas y mantienen el silencio. Al hablar abiertamente, combate el estigma y fomenta un cambio en la actitud hacia las sobrevivientes.

**Próximo paso** – Pratistha planea continuar su trabajo en salud mental en Australia y Nepal. Sus esfuerzos pueden inspirar a más sobrevivientes a buscar ayuda y hablar con libertad. Esto podría llevar a mejores sistemas de apoyo y voces más fuertes contra la violencia de género en el sur de Asia.

**Mensaje en una frase** – El camino de Pratistha Gautam de víctima a defensora muestra el poder del coraje y el cuidado para ayudar a las sobrevivientes a sanar y enfrentar el estigma.

articles.title: Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want
articles.summary: People say they often hear nothing back after applying for jobs. But could employers be forced to respond to every applicant?
articles.content:
Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a significant social issue—job applicant ghosting—that negatively impacts young jobseekers' mental health and employment prospects. The proposed policy recommendation to require large employers to provide meaningful feedback to all unsuccessful applicants under 25 represents a positive, actionable step toward improving transparency, dignity, and fairness in the hiring process. This has broad societal significance, particularly for youth employment and empowerment, and is supported by a major government review with measurable goals.
articles.personality_title: New rules may require employers to give job feedback to young applicants
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many young people applying for jobs in the UK often do not hear back from employers after interviews. This problem, called "job ghosting," leaves jobseekers feeling ignored and lowers their confidence.

**What happened** – A government review led by former minister Alan Milburn suggested that large employers should give clear feedback to all unsuccessful job applicants under 25. This idea aims to help young people understand why they were not hired and improve their chances in the future. The plan mostly applies to England but encourages other parts of the UK to adopt similar rules.

**Impact** – If employers start giving feedback, young jobseekers would feel more respected and less like "just a number." This could help them learn from their mistakes and stay motivated while looking for work. It also shows a new effort to make the hiring process fairer and more open.

**What's next step** – The government and employers will discuss how to put this feedback system in place. They will need to find ways to give responses without making the process too slow or difficult, especially since big companies get many applications.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new government proposal aims to make job hunting fairer by requiring large employers to explain to young applicants why they were not selected.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouvelles règles pourraient obliger les employeurs à donner un retour aux jeunes candidats
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – De nombreux jeunes au Royaume-Uni ne reçoivent souvent aucune réponse après un entretien d'embauche. Ce problème, appelé « ghosting » des candidats, les fait se sentir ignorés et baisse leur confiance en eux.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Une étude menée par l'ancien ministre Alan Milburn propose que les grandes entreprises donnent un retour clair à tous les candidats de moins de 25 ans non retenus. Cette idée vise à aider les jeunes à comprendre pourquoi ils n'ont pas été embauchés et à améliorer leurs chances à l'avenir. Le plan s'applique surtout en Angleterre, mais encourage les autres régions du Royaume-Uni à adopter des règles similaires.

**Impact** – Si les employeurs commencent à donner un retour, les jeunes candidats se sentiront plus respectés et moins comme « un simple numéro ». Cela pourrait les aider à apprendre de leurs erreurs et à rester motivés dans leur recherche d'emploi. Cela montre aussi un effort pour rendre le processus de recrutement plus juste et transparent.

**Prochaines étapes** – Le gouvernement et les employeurs vont discuter de la façon de mettre en place ce système de retour. Ils devront trouver des moyens de répondre sans ralentir ou compliquer le processus, surtout car les grandes entreprises reçoivent beaucoup de candidatures.

**En une phrase** – Une nouvelle proposition gouvernementale veut rendre la recherche d'emploi plus juste en obligeant les grandes entreprises à expliquer aux jeunes candidats pourquoi ils n'ont pas été choisis.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas reglas podrían exigir a los empleadores dar retroalimentación a jóvenes solicitantes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchos jóvenes que solicitan empleo en el Reino Unido a menudo no reciben respuesta después de las entrevistas. Este problema, llamado "ghosting" laboral, hace que los buscadores de empleo se sientan ignorados y pierdan confianza.

**Qué pasó** – Una revisión del gobierno liderada por el exministro Alan Milburn sugirió que las grandes empresas den retroalimentación clara a todos los solicitantes menores de 25 años que no sean seleccionados. Esta idea busca ayudar a los jóvenes a entender por qué no fueron contratados y mejorar sus oportunidades futuras. La propuesta se aplica principalmente en Inglaterra, pero anima a otras regiones a adoptar reglas similares.

**Impacto** – Si los empleadores comienzan a dar retroalimentación, los jóvenes se sentirán más respetados y no como "solo un número". Esto podría ayudarles a aprender de sus errores y mantener la motivación en la búsqueda de trabajo. También muestra un esfuerzo por hacer el proceso de contratación más justo y transparente.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno y los empleadores discutirán cómo implementar este sistema de retroalimentación. Necesitarán encontrar formas de responder sin hacer que el proceso sea lento o difícil, especialmente porque las empresas grandes reciben muchas solicitudes.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Una nueva propuesta del gobierno busca hacer la búsqueda de empleo más justa al exigir a las grandes empresas que expliquen a los jóvenes solicitantes por qué no fueron seleccionados.
